utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You can all be seated. We shall resume our hearing, and I will have the witness brought in. Good afternoon to the interpreters, good afternoon to the court reporters. Can the interpreters hear me? Yes. Very well. Good afternoon to the Defence counsel, to counsel for the Prosecution. (The accused/witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And good afternoon to the accused, who is presently a witness in this case. I am informing the public of this. This is now the cross-examination of Colonel Blaskic, now General Blaskic, and right now, the accused is a witness, and he now benefits from all the rights and duties of a witness testifying under oath. Mr. Kehoe is about to resume his cross-examination. Mr. Kehoe, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, Counsel. Good afternoon, General. If you could just take a second to gather your things, and we will commence when you are ready.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I am ready.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, we are going to shift gears now. General, we are going to talk about your period of time in Kiseljak and thereafter, beginning in April of 1992, and some of the events that took place in the Kiseljak municipality commencing in early April of 1992. What I would like you to look at is just review some documents quickly, and we will move through these documents quickly because we are most interested in the dates of these events because we have spoken about the contents previously, and with the permission of the usher, I would ask for Exhibits 406/5, 406/6, and Exhibit 583 be given to the defendant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, have you been given the whole of the documents that will be needed today?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, because I would like us to move forward as quickly as possible. You know, it is always time-consuming to deal with these documents, so we will try to be as quick as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, just going through the chronology of the events in early April of 1992, you testified that you left Zagreb to go to Kiseljak on the 6th of April, and as we can see from Prosecutor's Exhibit 406/5, Croatia recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 7th of April and also granted dual citizenship to Croatian citizens or Bosnian Croat citizens. Now, you also testified previously that on the 8th of April, the next day, the Croatian Defence Council or the HVO was established. Now, when you met Josip Boro for the first time, he told you that the municipal assembly had ceased to exist; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When I met the president of the municipal assembly for the first time, he said that the municipal assembly had, at a previous meeting, transferred all its competencies to the municipal crisis staff composed of Croatian and Muslim members and that for the time being the municipal assembly was not functioning. But it existed and it did not cease to exist. It ceased to function because of the war dangers and threats that existed in the region or the decisions by parliamentary representatives in the Kiseljak municipality. But I wasn't present at that particular meeting. I think it occurred at the beginning of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would the date 9 April, 1992 refresh your recollection as the date when the last session of the municipal assembly of Kiseljak took place?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that time, I had been taken prisoner by the Yugoslav army, but at all events, I don't question the date at all. I know that it was the beginning of April 1992. I don't think it was the last meeting of the municipal assembly of Kiseljak but that it was a meeting at which the municipal crisis staff was nominated, composed of Croatian and Muslim representatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if a prior witness testified that the last session of the municipal assembly was, in fact, on the 9th of April, 1992, you would have no reason to question that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would have reason in saying that the last -- using the term "the last session" because in August 1992, I attended a meeting of the municipal assembly of Kiseljak, and that is why I would have reason to do this because it wasn't the last. Perhaps it was the last in April. There, I agree. Because in April, I don't know that there were any more meetings after that. But, Your Honours, I was not a member of the municipal assembly of Kiseljak at all. I was never a member of the crisis staff of Kiseljak municipality, and I did not take part in decision-making of the crisis staff in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Without belabouring the point, Mr. President, the actual testimony concerning the date of the 9th of April of 1992 is on page 8086, lines 2 through 4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, let us move to the next document, and this is 406/6, a document that we discussed before, which is the next day, the 10th of April, 1992, and this is the document where President Tudjman orders General Bobetko to go to the southern front as the commander of all units on the southern front. You will recall this document, I'm sure, General, and I'd like you to take a look at this document in conjunction with the next exhibit, Mr. Registrar, Prosecutor's Exhibit 583.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If I may just make a comment with regard to document 406/6 (sic), a very brief comment, Your Honours? In point 2 of the document, of document 406/6, it says that dual citizenship is being offered to the members of the Croatian people and it proposes that this question be regulated by a bilateral agreement probably between the two presidents, that is to say, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and the president of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, and I understand point 2 -- perhaps I have understood that point incorrectly, but I understand it is a subject to be discussed and agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for the record, General, I think counsel will agree, that is Prosecutor's Exhibit -- the document you were referring to on dual citizenship is, in fact, Prosecutor's Exhibit 406/5 and not 406/6. I say that not to correct your testimony but simply to make the record as accurate as possible. So, General, let us look at the next exhibit, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 583, which is also a document dated the 10th of April, the same day that Tudjman orders Bobetko to the southern front, and this particular order, we have discussed before, is the order from President Mate Boban where he orders, at the bottom of the page: "Croatian Defence Council. This body is the only legal one, and only this name is official." Go to the bottom, Mr. Usher, if you can pull that all of the way up? "The HVO has its Main Staff. The HVO has Municipal Staffs in all the municipalities of the (Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna). Starting today, 10 April 1992 the HVO Main Staff will communicate only with the municipal staffs of the HVO. "All other military formations in the territory of the (Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna) are either illegal or hostile. All other names will be removed from official use." So, General, two days after the establishment of the HVO, Tudjman has deployed General Bobetko of the Croatian army to the southern front and President Boban has ordered that all military formations other than the HVO are illegal in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, in connection with these documents, I can say that on the 8th of April, 10th of April, I was captive. I think that I was at the Tuzla garrison at the time. I had been taken prisoner by the Yugoslav army. But my comment is that the HVO was set up on the 8th of April, and this organisational order, that is to say, document 583, issued by Mr. Boban, quite obviously did not -- the situation on the terrain did not correspond to what was said here because there were armed groups there and all that was when the Yugoslav People's Army in Bosnia-Herzegovina was the only legal armed force which had undertaken combat operations against the Croatian and Muslim people in the region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, when you met Josip Boro in Kiseljak on 14 April, 1992, did he inform you about what had been happening concerning the establishment of the HVO and the dispensing of the municipal assembly and the movement of Bobetko to the southern front and the outlawing of the TO in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna? Did he inform you of all those things during your first meeting?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already talked about what he told me. I would have to consult my notes again if I were to repeat in detail what we discussed. He didn't tell me anything about General Bobetko. I remember him telling me about the formation of the municipal crisis staff and he informed me that the municipal crisis staff was at the head of life in the community and the municipality, he said that the JNA garrison was still located in Kiseljak, he also told me that there was an army, that is to say, the Yugoslav People's Army, in Kiseljak, and we also discussed preparations for the defence of the municipality of Kiseljak. As to the other details, if you want to know in detail everything he told me, I would have to consult my chronology and notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, you can consult your notes any time that you feel the need to do so. I will ask you with regard to your conversation with Boro, did he tell you that in the municipal assembly that the Croats did not have an absolute majority?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, about any kind of absolute majority, as far as I remember, because I didn't talk to him, I'm only relying on my memory, I've already told this Honourable Trial Chamber that I have no great experience at the work of civilian authorities in my previous life, neither did I have contact with the civilian authorities. I only did as a citizen, and I was an active military man. Now, how many representatives in the municipal parliament there were, he did not say and I did not discuss the matter with him, but I do remember that he told me that the municipal crisis staff was composed of the Croatian-Muslim representatives appointed by the municipal assembly of Kiseljak and that there was a certain proportion to representation, a certain proportion of Croatians and Muslim Bosniaks in that crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that a majority is above 50 per cent, isn't it? Fifty-one per cent is a majority, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I know that a majority is above 51 per cent, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Bosnian Croats in the municipal assembly did not have 51 per cent of the seats prior to the dispensing of the assembly; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Perhaps it is. If you have some facts and figures I can comment on them, but in 1975, the academic year of 1975, I left the municipality of Kiseljak. And I had no previous contacts. I didn't even know Josip Boro. I didn't have any personal contacts with him. I was in Belgrade doing my education and then I served in Slovenia. But if you have facts on this, then quite possibly that is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, did you attend any of the crisis staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I attended several meetings when I was ordered to do so. That is to say, when they asked me to attend. I did not have the right of decision-making at those meetings, I just had the possibility of informing the crisis staff, municipal crisis staff, on those questions that they were interested in. As I was not a member of the crisis staff, I was not able to take part in any decision-making on whatever matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, within the crisis staff in the meetings that you attended, General, it's true that there were nine Croat votes and six Muslim votes; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Possibly that was the ratio, yes. I was usually with Mr. Bakir Alispahic at the meetings, but at all events I do know that there were a little more Croats compared to the Bosniak Muslims, and I know at least two of the Bosniak Muslims who attended those meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So based on your experience at those meetings, General, any vote between the Croats and the Muslims along ethnic lines would be won by the Croats; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the municipality of Kiseljak that is correct. If a decision was taken by voting and if nine Croats were in favour and six Bosniak Muslims did not, then the decision was passed on the basis of that result.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's move ahead with what is happening in the Kiseljak municipality after you arrive on the 14th or after your discussion with Josip Boro on the 14th of April of 1992. I ask you to take a look at Prosecutor's Exhibit 314 first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do believe there is a French copy available, as well as an English. Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have a French version before me, Mr. Kehoe. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This particular document is dated the 23rd of April of 1992 and, General, that is the day, is it not, where you were appointed commander of the armed formations of the municipal crisis staff of Kiseljak, isn't it? Take your time, General. Gather yourself and take your time.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You tell me when you're ready, General.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Would you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly. I'm focusing on the date of this document, on the date of Prosecutor's Exhibit 314. Prosecutor's Exhibit 314 takes place on the 23rd of April 1992, and that is the date you are appointed commander of the armed formations by the municipal crisis staff of Kiseljak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, I was appointed on the 23rd of April, together with Mr. Bakir Alispahic, by the municipal crisis staff of Kiseljak, although, that meeting was interrupted because there was an unexpected withdraw by the Yugoslav People's Army from the Kiseljak garrison. The command of the garrison, his name was Colonel Kosovac, that was his surname, I don't know his name, sent a demand to the president of the municipal crisis staff that he should urgently come to the barracks to meet him, and the meeting was interrupted and I did not take part in the continuation of the meeting. But the date is the correct date and I was appointed together with Mr. Bakir Alispahic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Generally speaking, General, would you try to answer more quickly and more precisely? I seem to understand that Mr. Kehoe is asking you whether from the 23rd of April onwards you took the head of the military crisis staff that was functioning in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Mr. President, but not only me but I, together with this other man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, nine days after you first meet Josip Boro, you are in charge of the military formations for the HVO; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I became commander of the armed forces, and I already said together with Mr. Bakir Alispahic at a meeting of the municipal crisis staff which was attended both by Croatian and Muslim members of the municipal crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, on that same day, if you look at Exhibit 314, we have a decision by that crisis staff which notes that: "The HVO headquarters for the area of the Kiseljak municipality shall be formed." Now, this particular event takes place -- this setup of the HVO headquarters in Kiseljak, in conjunction with your appointment, takes place approximately two weeks or a little bit more than two weeks after the HVO was formed, it being formed on the 8th of April, 1992; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The Croatian Defence Council was founded on the 8th of April, 1992. This Exhibit 314, it says in the preamble, "On the basis of Article 7 of the Kiseljak municipality Statute," and it was a decision of the municipal crisis staff, of which I was not a member. It is true that this was about 14 or 15 days after the HVO was formed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These particular HVO headquarters were formed during this time frame all over the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. As far as I can remember, that depended from one municipality to the next. It was formed over a certain period of time, but that depended on the situation in each municipality because the times were such it wasn't formed throughout the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna on this date. In some places earlier on, in others later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it all took place around the same period of time, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I know for certain that, for instance, in Novi Travnik, the headquarters was formed much later. This may have been in May already. But in any event, it was roughly at the same time. It depended from one municipality to the next. As I've already said, the municipalities were left to their own resources, and these municipal crisis staffs were formed at the municipal assemblies, and it depended on conditions. In places where the front lines were with the Serbs and the Yugoslav People's Army, they were formed earlier on. Where there was no contact, somewhat later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, your appointment on the 23rd of April, as well as the setting up of the HVO headquarters in Kiseljak, were the first steps by the HVO to take over the entire municipality; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My appointment I understood to be on behalf of the municipal assembly of Kiseljak, that is, by all members of the Kiseljak parliament. The appointment, on the basis of that decision, was carried out by the municipal crisis staff, and I focused on my military assignments. We see here that it was a decision of the municipal crisis staff, taken probably in accordance with the rules of procedure of the crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, were the Muslims happy with your selection?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that no one who attended that meeting had any opposition to my nomination. I listened to them. I didn't know them in person earlier on, hardly any one of them, and not one of them expressed any kind of a negative reaction or opposition to the proposal for my nomination. What is more, in April I met with Muslim priests, and judging by their reactions at those meetings, I never noticed that any one of them might have been dissatisfied with my election.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about some negative reactions to some of your actions, and we'll start first on the 24th of April, with Prosecutor's Exhibit 316. Now, General, this is a document received in evidence, which is an order that takes place the next day, 24th of April, 1992, and a commission was set up to compile an inventory list of the weapons in the Kiseljak barracks. Do you recall this particular order and your participation in the compilation of this inventory?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly. This was just one day after entry into the barracks. Already the next day, the municipal crisis staff took the decision that an inventory be made of the whole Kiseljak barracks and I was a member of that commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people on this commission were Croats and how many Muslims?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Three are Croats and two are Bosniak Muslim members of this commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the plan was that these weapons were going to be distributed to both the Muslims and the Croats; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We are talking about this document now, and this is a document on a list of the inventory, not of weapons. There was another document issued also by the municipal crisis staff, and again the commission consisted of both Croats and Muslims, regarding the distribution of weapons. As for this document, we made an inventory of everything, including weapons, that were to be found in the barracks but all the other equipment as well. So let me just mention an example. In one building, we would take note of the number of beds, the number of switches, the number of lamps. Therefore, a total inventory of immovable property that was in the barracks was something that we had to make a list of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, let's focus on the weapons. There was supposed to be a distribution of the weapons by ethnic lines, isn't that right, along ethnic lines?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wouldn't quite agree that it was to be along ethnic lines but, in any event, the weapons were distributed on the basis of a decision of the crisis staff, according to which two members of the HVO and members of the TO or the Patriotic League, but the HVO also had some Bosniak Muslims, some Serbs, and some Croats. In those days, there were also some members who were Romanies or Gypsies. And also within Territorial Defence ranks there were some Croats and also in the Patriotic League. Therefore, the weapons were to be distributed on the basis of the decision of the municipal crisis staff. This commission also covered or checked the warehouse where the weapons were stored.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, shortly after this particular inventory was to be made, didn't the Muslims protest publicly in downtown Kiseljak because the distribution wasn't made?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what the motives behind the protest were. In those days, there were very many incidents. Already on the 26th of April, the neighbouring municipality of Busovaca was shelled by the air force of the Yugoslav People's Army; then there were also problems within Kiseljak municipality of armed groups of criminals. Perhaps you could be more specific regarding the time too?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I am trying all the time to speed up things a little. If you have the feeling that there was a public protest against the distribution of weapons, I think it would be better if you were to say, "I submit that there was a public protest," and give the argument. This way you say, "Was there a public protest?" and then the witness says, "I'm not sure what the reasons were," and so on. And then eventually you will come to your argument. I think that we should try to be a little more efficient, if possible. If you, the Prosecution, know and are sure that there was a public protest against the distribution of arms, you should say so, and the witness will tell you if he doesn't agree. This way, we'll never get through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If I could go into a private session just briefly for this portion of the transcript, we can get through this quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: For the benefit of the public gallery, I should like to say that in order to protect testimony provided during the proceedings in closed session, we have to go into a private session for a short time to review that testimony. So let's go into private session. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: redacted pages 21152-21156 – private session 1 (redacted) 2 (redacted) 3 (redacted) 4 (redacted) 5 (redacted) 6 (redacted) 7 (redacted) 8 (redacted) (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are we in public session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We're in public session now, Mr. Prosecutor. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, let us talk about -- you noted just previously some of the protests by the Bosnian Muslims, and I'd like you to look at Prosecutor's Exhibit 315.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If we're not going to talk about the distribution of weapons, Mr. President, may I just say that the weapons were distributed according to a decision of the municipal crisis staff, but the problem was in having lists to see who had got the weapons. The municipal crisis staff, as far as I know, never received a list about how many weapons had been distributed and to who among the Territorial Defence and that was where the problem lay, in these lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, General, for these details. That's fine. We are now looking at Prosecution Exhibit 315.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in Prosecution's Exhibit 315, the municipal crisis staff transferred the Kiseljak barracks, which was the former JNA barracks, to the HVO, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says in this decision. The municipal crisis staff, probably at its meeting, made a decision of this kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You moved your office in there; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had an office in the barracks in Kiseljak and I shared it with Mr. Bakir Alispahic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will talk about Bakir Alispahic in a bit, sir, but this particular barracks was now controlled totally by the HVO; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. The HVO and the Patriotic League. The Patriotic League had its office at the barracks. It had its logistics man. It used part of the facilities in the Dalmatia Hotel. So the HVO and the Patriotic League used the same barracks. The members Patriotic League were, for the most part, Bosniak Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that Bakir Alispahic was a member of the Patriotic League? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that time, that is how he -- what he said, and he worked on their behalf. At that time, I cooperated with him and considered him to be a member of the Patriotic League because that is how he introduced himself. I don't know the overall organisational set up of the Patriotic League, and I don't know who determined and in what way the -- appointed the commanders of the Patriotic League and what the personal relationships were within the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it likewise your testimony, General, that when the Patriotic League merged into the Territorial Defence that Bakir Alispahic also joined the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know who he merged with, but I maintain that I cooperated throughout, while I was in Kiseljak, with Mr. Bakir Alispahic, that I visited members of the Patriotic League whenever they asked me to do so. I had meetings with them as well. I also claim that at the Dalmatia Hotel in Kiseljak they had an equal number of rooms at their disposal as did the members of the HVO, that is to say, one floor was used by them. I think it was the third floor of the hotel, but that's not an important point. Another floor was used by the HVO. The rest were Bosniak Muslims, refugees from Rakovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have noted several times to this Trial Chamber, in response to questions by my learned colleague, about your cooperation with Bakir Alispahic. Bakir Alispahic was never the commander of the Territorial Defence, was he?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know Bakir Alispahic from the Patriotic League. I never claimed that he was the commander of the Territorial Defence. I didn't consider him to be the commander of the Territorial Defence, but I did consider him to be, and that is how he induced himself, as commander of the Patriotic League, the military formation set up by the Party of Democratic Action, which was a majority Bosniak Muslim party in Kiseljak at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, Bakir Alispahic was working with you in conjunction with a man by the name of Suad Curic who is also known as Sok; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. The two of them worked together. There was another man, another commander. He was from Tulica. His surname was Barjaktarevic. I'm not quite sure what his name was. I think it was Esref. And, of course, the lower down commanders from the Patriotic League, a number of them who cooperated and worked together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in mid April of 1992, President Izetbegovic ordered that all military formations merge into the Territorial Defence, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Possibly an order of that kind was issued. I personally did not have it in my hands, but quite possibly an order of that kind had been issued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That merger included merging the Patriotic League into the Territorial Defence, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would like you to show me a document to see what it states and what is maintained in the document. If you say that is so, probably it is, but I never saw a document to that effect, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we can read you some testimony in that regard, General, but let me ask you some additional questions in this area. After President Izetbegovic ordered that the Patriotic League merge into the Territorial Defence, several Muslims, including Bakir Alispahic and Suad Curic, chose not to join the Territorial Defence and, rather, decided to cooperate with you and the HVO; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't like that, because the Patriotic League cooperated throughout. I would have to look at my notes in greater detail, but I had meetings with those personnel and with that unit, and we had cooperation throughout the time that I was in Kiseljak. So it wasn't only Bakir Alispahic who remained, their soldiers remained as well, as did their obligations and everything we did. So not only Bakir and Suad Curic, but there was Barjaktarevic and the other commanders of the Patriotic League as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When this occurred, General, while you were in Kiseljak, the commander of the Territorial Defence was not Bakir Alispahic but Sead Sinanbasic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sead Sinanbasic was a member of the municipal crisis staff, as far as I recall, by virtue of his function, and he was the commander of the municipal staff for Territorial Defence of Kiseljak. That is what he was since the time of the elections. Tomo Trutina was the crisis staff and commander of the Croatian Defence Council within the municipal crisis staff in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to be very clear, General, there was a group that Sok and Bakir Alispahic were in that was cooperating with you and the HVO, and there was the Territorial Defence, whose commander was Sead Sinanbasic; isn't that right? Two separate groups.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, there were many groups of armed individuals. I don't know what period you have in mind, but what you say is correct. Let me add that there was also HOS, there was the Vrazja Divizija, there were members of the Black Swans, there were other criminal groups in Kiseljak, the active component of MUP, the reserve component of MUP. Each village had its armed formation, armed group, which did not always reflect the ethnic composition. It was just an armed group of that particular village. So as I say, there were a number of armed groups, not only the Territorial Defence on the one hand and the HVO and the Patriotic League on the other. And there was a lot of fluctuation in manpower, so that one day someone would be a member of the Territorial Defence and the next day he would come and be a member of the HVO. So those were the beginnings of all this setup, at the earliest period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you said there were other criminal groups in Kiseljak. Sead Sinanbasic and the Territorial Defence were not one of those criminal groups, were they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My comment was concerned with the armed groups. Of course, Sead Sinanbasic and the Territorial Defence was not a criminal group in the sense of crime, perpetrators of crime. I spoke about armed groups or armed formations, armed villagers in the municipality of Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us go back to the JNA barracks, which is now the HVO barracks. Did Sead Sinanbasic have an office with you in the Kiseljak barracks?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He did not have it together with me, but he did together with Tomo Trutina, as far as I remember. That was in the building of the former municipal secretariat for national defence. That is what the plaque on the wall outside still said. If you have a model, I can point out the building to you, because Sead Sinanbasic was the counterpart of Tomo Trutina and he was on the same level, and I was a subordinate in the HVO to Tomo Trutina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the building you evicted Sead Sinanbasic from on 14th of May, 1992, after the TO was outlawed; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Are you talking about the 14th of May?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the 14th of May of 1992. The HVO evicted Sead Sinanbasic and the Territorial Defence from the building that you just described, the secretariat for national defence; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is absolutely incorrect. He returned them to that building, that is to say, he asked them to go back to the building. So that is not correct. On that particular night, the 14th of May, perhaps it was between 20.00 or 21.00, they returned, and perhaps I will say something wrong there, but I think it was building 3 and the TO section there. I know the event you're talking about, but I think it would take a long time for me to explain, but if you want to I shall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Explain it to the Judges. I mean, if you're talking about cooperating with the Territorial Defence, what was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a second. You can ask for precisions when you put precise questions to the witness. We are losing time which is bad for the Defence, for the Prosecution, and for the justice in general. We the Judges are here to ensure that the trial can go forward in conditions of total equity so that everybody can speak up. So, yes, it's nice to go into explanations and details but you have, Mr. Kehoe, to put precise questions to the witness. You said on May 14th the HVO evicted Mr. Sinanbasic. Do you have arguments to support this? Can you expose them to the witness? This will allow the witness to answer you in a precise way and to ensure that all his rights are protected. Right now we're going to take a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Please be seated. I suggest we work for about 30 minutes. Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If I could just go into private session briefly for some closed session testimony? (Private session) 17 (redacted) 18 (redacted) 19 (redacted) 20 (redacted) 21 (redacted) 22 (redacted) 23 (redacted) 24 (redacted) 25 (redacted) redacted page 21167-21169 – private session 1 (redacted) 2 (redacted) 3 (redacted) 4 (redacted) 5 (redacted) 6 (redacted) 7 (redacted) 8 (redacted) 9 (redacted) 10 (redacted) 11 (redacted) 12 (redacted) 13 (redacted) 14 (redacted) 15 (redacted) 16 (redacted) 17 (redacted) 18 (redacted) 19 (redacted) (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This group, General, with Bakir Alispahic and Suad Curic, is the group that had an office and facilities in the Kiseljak barracks; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, in the facilities of the Kiseljak barracks, after HVO units entered, there were also units of the Patriotic League while I was commander in Kiseljak of the armed formations in Kiseljak. There was not a group -- allow me to explain. It is true that Suad Curic was there and that the main commander was Bakir Alispahic, a commander of a military formation; Esref Barjaktarevic, a native of Tulica; and at all times there were about 30 mobile armed soldiers accommodated in the Dalmatia Hotel in Kiseljak, together with an equal number of HVO soldiers who were accommodated in a similar fashion, as I have already explained. And if I may comment on what the Prosecutor has just read out? I was not a member of the Patriotic League, and it is possible that Mr. Izetbegovic did address an order to the Patriotic League, or I don't know whom, but I have just remembered that Suad Curic told me on one occasion that he had problems with the Kiseljak SDA which wanted to abolish them. Regarding apartments, as mention was made here of apartments, Hajro Hajdarevic, we called him "Hajro," he was the commander of a TO detachment, he also used an apartment, Bakir was given an apartment by the municipal crisis staff, a commander from the Kiseljak garrison, Mr. Mustafa Polutak, retained his apartment even after the Yugoslav army had left Kiseljak. And I cooperated with the Territorial Defence. I had quite a number of meetings. Let me mention one held on the 5th of June at the command post called Mokrine -- there is no relief for me to show you -- I met with a commander of the Territorial Defence detachment and we jointly prepared an operation to lift the blockade of Sarajevo, and he informed me of all the assignments linked to that operation. I also toured virtually all the villages of Bosnian Muslims in Kiseljak municipality and I personally never had any problems nor did I notice any negative reactions nor was I received negatively by Bosniak Muslims. It is true that the Patriotic League is a broader organisation. It held its meeting in February 1992 in Travnik, in the village of Mehuric, and at that meeting it was noted that it numbered between 60.000 and 70.000 men organised in 109 municipalities of Bosnia-Herzegovina with nine regional headquarters throughout the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, the Muslim entity that you -- Bosnian Muslim villages that you toured you toured with Bakir Alispahic not Sead Sinanbasic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not have such a position as to be able to tour the villages with Sead Sinanbasic. Tomislav Trutina may have toured the villages with him, but I toured the villages alone and also with Bakir. I also toured them with the head of the European Monitoring Mission, Mr. Fleming, and when he expressed surprise after the January conflict, I told him, Mr. Fleming, "You name the village. I will go with you. I don't need any security or protection." And wherever he wanted to go, I went with him myself, Mr. Fleming, his driver, to the villages that Mr. Fleming claimed were witnessing problems between Bosniak Muslims and Croats. On that occasion, I even visited Bosniak houses together with Mr. Fleming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, let me show you a document. Unfortunately, Mr. President, there is not a French copy of this yet. I will read just a portion of this document at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is Exhibit 631 and 631A for the English version, Prosecutor's Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, this is a document that is signed by Sead Sinanbasic on the 15th of May, 1992, noting at the top, "Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kiseljak Municipal Assembly, Territorial Defence Main Staff." We will read it through, General, because there is not a French copy at this point. The subject matter is "Information regarding the situation in Kiseljak Municipal Assembly," and it goes to the Republican Staff of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Territorial Defence. "1. On 14 May 1992, the Croatian Defence Council command banned the work of the command of the Kiseljak municipal (Territorial Defence) on the premises of the former JNA Hall and threatened to ban its work completely because only the HVO command existed on the territory of the municipality. The order was issued by Tihomir Blaskic, the commander of the Kiseljak Municipal Headquarters. "2. On the same day, TO units were denied passage and the possibility of operating against the enemy from our territory. Movement of TO units was also banned in these regions, without a special approval from the Main Headquarters. "3. TO units from neighbouring municipalities have been denied passage through our municipality, unless specifically approved by the Main Headquarters. "4. At a meeting of the Crisis Staff held on 14 May 1992 at 2100 hours it was concluded that the HVO Main Headquarters had not issued approval for planned combat operations with the purpose of assisting Sarajevo because the Crisis Staff of the Kiseljak municipality, apparently, does not have such competence. "5. At the meeting of the Crisis Staff it was concluded that the Kiseljak Municipal Assembly should be convened immediately." Now, while you are examining that document, General, I would like you to also look at Prosecutor's 502 which is your order of 11 May, 1992, outlawing the TO in the Kiseljak area.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can answer if I may comment on this order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can comment on both of them when we look at these in conjunction, General. 502, of course, is the order that we discussed at length previously, of 11 May, 1992, that was issued pursuant to an order by General Roso, where in point 1 you order that: "1. The only legal military units in Kiseljak municipality are HVO units. And in number 5: "5. By this order all orders of the Territorial Defence are rendered invalid and the TO in this area considered illegal." So, General, this Territorial Defence unit which you maintain you were cooperating with, you outlaw on the 11th of May and then you ban from operating and working in the former JNA army hall on the 14th of May, 1992; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Until the 14th of May, 1992, in Bosnia-Herzegovina there was the Yugoslav People's Army in existence, and also the component of the Territorial Defence of the Yugoslav People's Army. My father, personally, could have been mobilised to report to the municipality of Ilijas. From the municipality of Kiseljak, workers in the maintenance facility in Hadzici could also have been called up for mobilisation because that was their wartime assignment, which meant that they had to respond to this call-up and to go empty-handed under the control of the Serbs. From the municipality of Ilidza, workers who also had wartime assignments, for instance, the factory Bitumenka and others, also could have been called up by the former JNA requesting them to report to their wartime duties. I did write this order, Exhibit number 502, on the 11th of May, and it says: "On the basis of orders received from the main staff." But under item 5, it doesn't say that the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is illegal. Unfortunately, it doesn't even say the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But Exhibit 601, used by Mr. Sead Sinanbasic, in the heading, it says the "Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina," the one that used to be part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Regarding the incident of the 14th of May about which Mr. Sead Sinanbasic informs the republican staff of the Territorial Defence, in Exhibit 631, there are quite a number of incorrectnesses (sic). On the 14th of May, 1992, in Kiseljak, a number of incidents had occurred, that is, within the municipality of Kiseljak. Thus, for instance, there was a clash in the local community of Brestovsko among Croats themselves, two groups of Croats, and the dispute was over the sale of cigarettes. Then there was a clash between the Croatian villages of Donji Palez and Donje Podastinje. The reason was a barricade and the profit to be gained at that roadblock. There was an incident between the Territorial Defence and the civilian Croatian driver in the village of Hercezi. His name was Mirko Tuka. Mr. Tucinovic opened fire at him. Mr. Tucinovic being a member of the Territorial Defence, after carrying out control of the vehicle and the driver, and after the driver was told to move away from the checkpoint. The gravest incident that occurred in the town of Kiseljak itself where all members who were armed rallied, they were all from Kiseljak, and the reason was movement of forces of the Territorial Defence towards the city centre of Kiseljak from the direction of Visoko. There were two bus loads and one truck full of soldiers coming from the direction of Travnik and Busovaca. There were two buses from the direction of Bilalovac, a local community within Kiseljak municipality. There were movements of some troops from the direction of Fojnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is simply not responsive to the question, Mr. President. I don't mean to cut him off the point at this point, but it is not responsive to the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your permission, all this happened on the 14th of May, and the witness wanted to explain why he limited the movement of these armed units around town, because there was the threat of an outright conflict. This is at the core of this information by Sead Sinanbasic. The introduction may have been too lengthy but this is very relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nobilo, for your explanations, but I have already asked the witness to try and be concise in his answers in his own interests, because we wish this trial to end by the deadline we have set. If we're talking about a document that the Judges have regarding an incident, I understand that your client has to describe the context and I didn't interrupt him, but it does seem to me that your client should try to be more concise in his answers. It is in his interest, after all, because, after all, you will not have enough time at some point in time if he dwells excessively on one date. So I would like him to be precise and concise regarding the incident referred to in this document and the order that you issued.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wanted to make an introduction to point 2, but let me go back to point 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, but the introduction, in any language, is meant to introduce something in order to proceed very quickly to the body, to the main issue. So I think there is no need for this semantic clarification. So please try and answer now.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will try to be as brief as possible. Except from Fojnica, also from the direction of Kresevo, there were movements by the members of the Territorial Defence towards the town of Kiseljak. This resulted in general confusion in Kiseljak, fear and apprehension amongst citizens. At 18.00, I was in the local community of Brestovsko. I wasn't in Kiseljak at all. I was called by Mr. Tomislav Trutina, who told me that there were problems between the HVO and the TO, and that allegedly all these movements along the directions that I have mentioned had the aim of lifting the blockade of the town of Sarajevo. No operation was carried out for deblocking Sarajevo through Kobiljaca, Rakovica, and Ilidza where allegedly efforts were being made to lift the blockade of Sarajevo. When I reached Kiseljak, the town of Kiseljak, I immediately went towards the building where a part of the TO staff was housed, that is, not the building where Sead Sinanbasic and the TO were housed. That building was the JNA home in Kiseljak, and they were in the restaurant of the JNA hall. I don't know on the basis of whose decision. On the way to that building there were a large number of armed soldiers and civilians and these forces were confronting the building. On the one side were the TO and on the other HVO troops. Tomislav reacted more sharply than me, the commander of the municipal HVO staff of Kiseljak, saying, "Why are you causing problems again? Can't you see all the things that have happened?" There were some other rather sharp words spoken by Tomislav. I kept quiet. I saw Mr. Mustafa Polutak and Mr. Cilas. I didn't see Sead Sinanbasic there in person, but I know that (redacted) was not there because at that time they were holding a meeting of the crisis staff in the municipality of Kiseljak discussing these same problems. I went back and I learned, in the meantime, that the commander of the village of Parezevici, his nickname was Kopo, was wounded in front of this building where a part of the TO staff were housed. That is the JNA hall it was called, in Kiseljak. Then I said to Mr. Cilas, "It would be best if, in view of the overall situation, that is, one of the village commanders has already been wounded and night has already fallen, it would be best that you go back and that we all stay in one building until the crisis staff makes a decision." Sometime about 20.00 hours, Cilas came and from then on the municipal staff of the TO of Kislejak used the premises when you enter the TO building to the left-hand side and the HVO use the premises on the right-hand side. In the ground floor, there was the municipal communications centre of the municipal crisis staff. I don't exactly know how the premises were distributed on the floors above. This incident was also discussed by the municipal crisis staff. As for this order, I was not the commander of the municipal staff of the HVO Kiseljak. That position was held by Tomislav Trutina. As regards point 2, in this document 631, I made contact with the checkpoints from the direction of Visoko, and I asked that any one of the members of the TO forces who were moving towards Kiseljak tell me who was in command of the operation for lifting the blockade of Sarajevo and who would be the commander of such an operation rallying so many troops. No one among them introduced himself, nor did they want to talk to me. I made the same request in the direction of Raskrsce. This is an area linked to Fojnica and Travnik and, also, Kresevo. I would have gladly spoken to any one of those commanders but not one of them wanted to give me any information. If they had called me to discuss the lifting of the blockade of Sarajevo, I would have gone. These forces, which didn't wish to say whether they had a commander or not, at 20.00 in the evening could not be allowed in Kiseljak municipality to carry out this operation of deblocking in Kiseljak, because this is a valley where such an operation was never conducted. It's not logical to go through a valley surrounded by hills. As for banning passage of TO units from neighbouring municipalities without any announcement, because there were cases when the soldiers of the Republika Srpska army wandered into the municipality, or other armed groups, so we wanted to have some kind of control over this large number of armed groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If I understand you well, General, I see that you are commenting on document 631 by giving us details on the context on the combat operations which took place and which constituted the very beginning of the hostilities. I see that you want us to interpret this document in light of these events. But, first of all, could you confirm whether or not you signed the order that was issued on the 11th of May, document 502A? This is from you.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Right. Do you have any other comment you wish to make on document 631A?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In point 4, it says that a meeting of the crisis staff was held, the municipal crisis staff of Kiseljak municipality. I really cannot remember which decisions the municipal crisis staff took, but I know that the Territorial Defence staff of Kiseljak municipality continued operating in the same building in which HVO members were housed and the same applied to August 1992. That is as much as I can say at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You have been able to say all you wanted to say. Mr. Kehoe, do you have a question that you want to put to the witness, other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have other questions, Mr. President. The question that I wanted to ask was the question that you asked, Mr. President, and I would move into another particular area. I don't know if Your Honour wants me to continue into that other area or break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, we are going to stop right here, but I would like us to go into private session for a short while, please. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: redacted page 21186 – 21187 – private session 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
